summary: Describes how an L2TP access concentrator can relay PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) discovery packets across an L2TP tunnel. This lets a customer on an Ethernet link find and connect to a remote provider's server, as if directly attached to it.

eli5.summary: A friend shouts "Who can help me?" in a room, and a messenger carries the shout through a tunnel to a faraway room where the helper answers.

questions: how does pppoe work over l2tp
subtitle: Relaying PPPoE service discovery across L2TP tunnels

tldr.problem: PPPoE hosts on an Ethernet link need to discover and connect to PPPoE access concentrators, but when the concentrator is reached via an L2TP tunnel, the discovery messages (which travel outside PPP) cannot cross the tunnel.
tldr.mechanism: L2TP defines two new control messages (SRRQ and SRRP) and a PPPoE Relay AVP that carries entire PPPoE Active Discovery packets through the L2TP control channel, relaying discovery negotiations between the host and a distant access concentrator.
tldr.outcome: Applications can offer transparent PPPoE service discovery and connection to remote providers over L2TP tunnels without changes to the PPP data plane, using the reliable L2TP control channel for discovery.

today: RFC 3817 is an Internet Standard Informational document. It remains the specification for relay of PPPoE Active Discovery across L2TP tunnels and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem: Discovery Across Tunnels
sections.content:
The PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) protocol allows a host on an Ethernet link to establish a PPP session with a distant server via L2TP. However, PPPoE defines a discovery phase (using PADI, PADO, PADR, and PADS messages) that happens before the PPP session starts. These discovery messages are not carried inside PPP, so they cannot tunnel with the PPP data frames over L2TP: the discovery negotiation must complete on the local Ethernet link, preventing the host from reaching a distant provider's access concentrator.

This document solves the problem by relaying these discovery packets through L2TP's control channel, preserving the discovery mechanism end-to-end while keeping PPP data transfer unchanged.
sections.eli5: Imagine meeting someone in person before getting their phone number. This RFC lets you ask "who's there?" and have someone on the far end hear your question and answer back, via a secure tunnel.

sections.title: How the Relay Works
sections.content:
When a LAC (L2TP Access Concentrator) receives a PPPoE Active Discovery Initiation (PADI) packet from a host, it packages the entire Ethernet frame into a PPPoE Relay AVP and sends it to the LNS (L2TP Network Server) via a new Service Relay Request (SRRQ) message on the established L2TP control connection.

The LNS processes or relays the PADI to a PPPoE access concentrator, which responds with a PADO. The PADO is carried back in a Service Relay Reply (SRRP) message. The LAC receives the PADO, updates the MAC address if needed, and forwards it to the PPPoE host on the local Ethernet link. When the host sends a Active Discovery Request (PADR) to select a service, the LAC creates an L2TP Incoming Call Request (ICRQ) with the PADR in the PPPoE Relay AVP. From this point on, the LNS uses the L2TP session itself to carry the final discovery messages (PADS and PADT) and then the PPP data.
sections.eli5: First, the messenger carries "Who's out there?" through the tunnel. The answerer shouts back "I'm here!", and the messenger brings the answer back. Then the message sender picks one, and they talk directly through the tunnel from then on.

sections.title: L2TP Messages and AVPs
sections.content:
This RFC defines two new L2TP control message types: Service Relay Request Message (SRRQ, message type 18) and Service Relay Reply Message (SRRP, message type 19). These messages carry a new PPPoE Relay AVP (attribute type 55) which encapsulates the complete PPPoE PAD message, including the Ethernet MAC header.

Two capability AVPs allow peers to negotiate support: the PPPoE Service Relay Response Capability AVP (attribute type 56) signals that a node can receive and process SRRQ/SRRP messages, and the PPPoE Service Relay Forward Capability AVP (attribute type 57) signals that a node can send them. These are exchanged during L2TP control connection setup. The M bit on these AVPs can require that the peer understand them before the connection is established.
sections.eli5: These are the new signals that say "I can carry messages through the tunnel for you" and the format for wrapping the discovery packet inside the tunnel message.

sections.title: Tracking Requests Across Relays
sections.content:
When a PADI is relayed through multiple nodes, each must track which PADO response belongs to which request. PPPoE defines two tags for this: the Host-Uniq TAG (a value the host picks) and the AC-Cookie TAG (a value the access concentrator picks). These tags must be echoed in any reply message.

The relay protocol uses a key rule: for messages traveling upstream (from host toward the access concentrator), each relaying node inserts a new Host-Uniq TAG before forwarding; for messages traveling downstream (from the access concentrator back), each node inserts a new AC-Cookie TAG. By encoding the next hop's identity into these tags (with encryption and authentication), a node can identify where to forward the response without storing state for every request. The PADS and PADT messages do not rely on these tags because they are carried within the L2TP session itself, where the session ID provides the necessary coherency.
sections.eli5: Each relay adds its own label to the message so it knows where to send the answer when it comes back. It's like each person in a chain adding their name to the message.

sections.title: Session Establishment and Teardown
sections.content:
Once a host sends a Active Discovery Request (PADR), the LAC stops relaying individual packets and instead treats the request as the start of an L2TP session. The LAC sends an ICRQ to the LNS with the PADR in the PPPoE Relay AVP. If the LNS approves the service, it responds with an Incoming Call Reply (ICRP) containing the Active Discovery Session-confirmation (PADS) message. The LAC inserts a valid PPPoE SESSION_ID, sends the PADS to the host, and completes the L2TP session with an Incoming Call Connected (ICCN) message. PPP data can then flow between the host and the LNS.

When the session ends, either party can initiate a Call Disconnect Notify (CDN) message carrying the Active Discovery Terminate (PADT) in the PPPoE Relay AVP. If the LNS initiated the disconnect, it sends a PADT in the CDN; if the host initiated it, the LAC sends the host's PADT to the LNS in the CDN. If the LAC receives an L2TP disconnect with no PADT, it generates and sends a properly formatted PADT to the host.
sections.eli5: Once the host picks a service, the tunnel stays open and carries all their conversation. When either one is done, they send a goodbye message that closes both the local connection and the tunnel.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
PPPoE service discovery information (service names, host identities) is normally visible only on the local Ethernet link. This RFC extends the discovery path through L2TP tunnels, potentially making this information visible to eavesdroppers on the tunnel path. An untrusted network may observe which services a host seeks or which identifiers it uses.

The RFC recommends two protections when the discovery information is sensitive. AVP hiding (defined in RFC 2661) encrypts the contents of the PPPoE Relay AVP in transit, though it provides no integrity check. The stronger method is to protect the L2TP tunnel itself with IPsec, which provides both confidentiality and integrity for all control and data traffic. Either measure should be used if the service discovery information could be sensitive.
sections.eli5: The messages travel through an extra tunnel now, so more people might see what the host is looking for. Wrapping the messages in extra locks (encryption) before they travel helps keep them secret.
